sources.title: Book request #184: 'Nix from First Principles' syllabus and editorial principles
Dolstra, The Purely Functional Software Deployment Model (2006)
Software Sustainability Institute: Reproducible Environments With Nix
Home Manager docs: Nix Flakes (mirror of nix-flakes.adoc)
DEV Community: overview of Nix, NixOS, Nixpkgs

structure.rationale: The order follows the requester's syllabus and its central question — how a description becomes a package, a dev environment, or a system. It goes: motivation and map, the store, the language, derivations and the build lifecycle, packaging and customization, dev environments and flakes, real applications and CI, then modules, Home Manager and NixOS (kept optional until late), and finally debugging, a capstone and contributing. Each chapter keeps the requester's seven-beat rhythm. Note: web fetches (nix.dev, Nix manual) were refused by the proxy during scaffolding, so no external sources were consulted yet; each concept page must fetch and record its sources before writing.
structure.audience: Developers comfortable with a terminal, git, one programming language and basic build/dependency workflows; no prior Nix or NixOS knowledge.

claims.text: Conventional package managers install into shared global locations (e.g. /usr/lib), so two programs needing different versions of one library compete for the same path; this is the 'dependency hell' Nix was designed to avoid.
Nix stores each package under a path containing a hash of all its inputs, so versions coexist side by side and upgrades/rollbacks are atomic.

Builds and install scripts often depend on undeclared things on the host (tools on PATH, system libraries, env vars, locale, OS version); these hidden assumptions are the usual cause of 'works on my machine'.

Recording what is installed (a snapshot such as pip freeze or a package list) lists results, not the inputs and steps that produced them, and usually omits the OS-level tools and libraries; a description states what should be present and how it is made.
Language lock files (mix.lock, Cargo.lock) pin language libraries but not the compiler, OS libraries or tools outside the language's package manager.
Nix builds run in a sandbox (default on Linux, not default on macOS) so undeclared dependencies fail loudly instead of silently working.

snippets.code: mix deps.get && mix phx.server   # assumes: Elixir, Erlang/OTP, a C compiler, Postgres client libs, inotify-tools already exist
snippets.note: illustrative hidden-assumption example for the book's Phoenix project; no Nix syntax in this chapter

pitfalls: Do not claim Nix makes everything perfectly reproducible; later chapters cover where it breaks down.
Do not show Nix syntax here; the chapter is motivation only.
Lock files help but only cover one layer.

claims.text: The word 'Nix' names several things: a purely functional language for describing builds, the package manager/build tool that evaluates it, and the culture around them; NixOS configuration is written in the same language.
The Nix package manager runs on Linux and other Unix-like systems (including macOS); NixOS is a full Linux distribution built on top of it, so NixOS is optional for using Nix.
Nixpkgs is the package collection: a very large set of package definitions, each written as a derivation-producing expression in the Nix language.
NixOS describes a whole operating system declaratively; configurations can be version-controlled and rolled back.
Home Manager manages user-level packages and dotfiles with Nix; it can run standalone (the only option on non-NixOS, non-nix-darwin systems) or as a module inside a NixOS or nix-darwin configuration.

Flakes are a project-level interface: a directory with flake.nix declaring inputs and outputs, with flake.lock pinning exact input revisions. They need the nix-command and flakes experimental features enabled and the docs still describe them as experimental.
Flakes were introduced with Nix 2.4.
Nix builds in a sandbox by default on Linux, which is why the store-and-derivation model is trusted for reproducibility.

snippets.note: illustrative; nix run needs nix-command and flakes enabled; first-run detail covered in chapter 3

pitfalls: 'Nix' is used for the language, the tool and loosely the whole ecosystem; always say which.
NixOS is not required to use Nix, Nixpkgs or Home Manager.
Do not treat flakes as a separate package manager; they are an interface over the same evaluation and build.
Mentioned names (nix-darwin, Cachix) are only pointers here; details come later.

claims.text: The recommended install on Linux and macOS is multi-user mode (a Nix daemon runs builds); the install command is: curl -L https://nixos.org/nix/install | sh -s -- --daemon.
Multi-user mode on Linux needs systemd with SELinux disabled; otherwise single-user install is the fallback. macOS is supported.
With the daemon, store-changing actions by an unprivileged user are forwarded to the Nix daemon.
Some macOS 15 Sequoia upgrades broke installs with a missing _nixbld group/user error (NixOS/nix issue #10892).
The installer accepts --help to list flags.
The `nix` command (nix run, nix shell, nix build, nix develop) needs nix-command (and for nixpkgs# references, flakes) experimental features enabled unless the installer enabled them.

`nix run nixpkgs#hello` fetches/builds the program into the store and runs it without adding it to your profile or PATH; `nix shell nixpkgs#cowsay` gives a subshell with the tool on PATH that disappears on exit.
`nix build` leaves a `result` symlink in the current directory pointing into /nix/store; it is a link, not a copy.
`nix develop` enters a development shell for a flake/derivation; `nix-shell -p` is the older equivalent for ad-hoc environments.

snippets.note: install command per nix.dev; version output varies
illustrative; one-off enabling; permanent: experimental-features = nix-command flakes in nix.conf (unsourced)

snippets.code:
nix shell nixpkgs#cowsay nixpkgs#lolcat
nix build nixpkgs#hello && ls -l result && ./result/bin/hello
snippets.note: unsourced, widely documented behaviour; the book tells the reader to check for themselves

pitfalls: Web fetches were refused by the proxy; several claims have no source and the page tells readers to verify by running.
Piping a script to sh: advise reading it first.
Flakes/nix-command wording is experimental; do not state stability firmly.
Exact output/store hashes differ per machine; do not print fake hashes as real.
Do not explain the store in depth; next chapter.
